title: sat-solver: a SAT solver from scratch in Rust, from DPLL to CDCL
summary: Boolean satisfiability, SAT for short, asks a simple question: given a formula over true/false variables, is there an assignment that makes it true? It is the textbook NP-complete problem, which is usually where the lesson stops. In theory it is hard. In practice, modern SAT solvers handle very large formulas, and they sit under package dependency resolvers, hardware verification tools and planners. The gap between "exponential in theory" and "works in practice" is filled by a handful of specific ideas. I wanted to understand them, so I wrote sat-solver : a boolean satisfiability solver from scratch in Rust, in two steps. First the classic DPLL algorithm, then CDCL (conflict-driven clause learning) in the style of MiniSat. It reads and writes DIMACS CNF and includes a Sudoku solver as a demo. It has no dependencies. This post is about what I built and what it teaches. What I built The formula representation. cnf.rs stores a formula in conjunctive normal form: a list of clauses, each a list of literals. A literal is packed into one integer as 2*var + sign , so a variable and its negation sit next to each other. The DIMACS parser handles comments, clauses that span several lines, and the SATLIB % end marker. DPLL, the baseline. dpll.rs is the classic algorithm: unit propagation to a fixpoint, branching on a literal from the shortest unsatisfied clause, and chronological backtracking. It is simple enough to trust, and that is its job here: it is the baseline the CDCL solver is checked against. CDCL, the real solver. cdcl.rs has the techniques that make modern solvers work: Two watched literals with blocker literals, so most satisfied clauses are skipped without touching clause memory. 1-UIP conflict analysis with local clause minimization, and non-chronological backjumping to the second-highest decision level in the learnt clause. VSIDS variable activity, kept in an indexed binary heap, plus phase saving. Luby restarts , with a unit of 100 conflicts. Learnt clause deletion : the less active half is dropped once the database passes a growing limit (binary and locked clauses are kept), and then garbage collected. Sudoku as a demo. sudoku.rs encodes a puzzle with 729 variables ("cell (r,c) holds d"), exactly-one constraints per cell, row, column and box, and the givens as unit clauses. is_unique blocks the first solution and solves again: if the second run is UNSAT, the puzzle has one solution. Instance generators. gen.rs produces pigeonhole formulas (UNSAT when there are more pigeons than holes), n-queens, and uniform random k-SAT. How to use it Clone the repository and build it. The binary is called sat . git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/sat-solver cd sat-solver cargo build --release S = target/release/sat $S solve tests/cnf/unsat_php_7_6.cnf # exit code 10 = SAT, 20 = UNSAT $S solve --dpll tests/cnf/sat_queens_10.cnf # use the DPLL baseline $S gen random 200 852 42 | $S solve - # random 3-SAT near the phase transition $S gen php 9 8 > php.cnf # pigeonhole instance (UNSAT) $S sudoku "8..........36......7..9.2...5...7.......457.....1...3...1....68..85...1..9....4.." Output follows the SAT competition format: an s SATISFIABLE line and v ... 0 lines with the model. Every model is checked against the formula before it is printed, so a "SAT" answer is never taken on faith. The third command is worth a closer look. gen random 200 852 42 makes a random 3-SAT formula with 200 variables and 852 clauses, using seed 42. The ratio of about 4.26 clauses per variable is the region where random 3-SAT is hardest, the phase transition. What I learned Learning from conflicts is the big idea. DPLL, when it hits a contradiction, undoes its last decision and tries the other value. It learns nothing, so it can hit the same contradiction again in another part of the search. CDCL asks why the conflict happened. It walks back through the implications to a clause that sums up the cause, adds that clause to the formula, and jumps back, often over several decisions that had nothing to do with the problem. The search never makes that mistake again. Most of the time is spent in propagation, so the data structure matters most. A naive solver visits every clause that contains a literal each time it is assigned. With two watched literals, a clause is only visited when one of its two watched literals becomes false, and nothing needs to be undone on backtracking. Blocker literals add a cheap check that often avoids opening the clause at all. Heuristics carry real weight. VSIDS bumps the activity of variables involved in recent conflicts, so the solver keeps working where the trouble is. Phase saving remembers the last value of each variable. Restarts abandon the current search path but keep the learnt clauses. None of these changes what the solver can prove. All of them change how long it takes. Forgetting is necessary. Learnt clauses pile up and slow propagation down. Dropping the less active half from time to time keeps the solver moving. A simple solver is the best test for a complex one. CDCL has many places for subtle bugs. Checking it against DPLL on random instances, and verifying every model, catches them. An encoding is a program too: writing the Sudoku constraints showed me how much of "using SAT" is choosing the variables well. Things to know This is a learning project. The README is specific about where it stands: On a laptop it solves random 3-SAT with 200 variables at the threshold in well under a second, but it is roughly an order of magnitude slower per conflict than MiniSat. It lacks recursive minimization, LBD-based clause management, preprocessing and inprocessing. There are no incremental assumptions. There is no proof output (DRAT), so UNSAT answers are not independently certified . Only SAT models are checked. What was tested. cargo test covers: the known instances in tests/cnf/ , where the file name prefix sat_ or unsat_ is the expected answer; pigeonhole from 3 pigeons in 2 holes up to 8 in 7; n-queens for n = 1 to 12, which is UNSAT exactly for n = 2 and 3; CDCL and DPLL agreeing on 150 random 3-SAT instances in the hard region, with every model verified; larger random instances; known Sudoku puzzles, including Arto Inkala's "hardest Sudoku", with their published solutions and uniqueness checks; the CLI's exit codes. Debug builds use smaller random instances. Run cargo test --release for the full sizes. Why I built it SAT solvers are a case where the engineering is as interesting as the theory. The algorithm on paper is short. What makes it work is a set of techniques that each sound minor and together change what is solvable. Reading about watched literals and 1-UIP learning does not show why they matter. Building DPLL first, then adding the CDCL parts one at a time, with the same instances to run at each step, makes the effect of each visible. Doing it in two steps also gave me a working oracle at every stage, which is the reason I trust the result as far as the tests go. Get the code The source, the test instances and the generators are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/sat-solver . It's MIT licensed. Issues and pull requests are welcome. Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz .

title: How I pull a vocal and a backing track out of one song
summary: When I want a karaoke track or a dry vocal from a finished mix, I go to Vocal Remover and upload the song there. The page splits the file into two pieces: the instrumental with the singing removed, and the vocal on its own. I have used both outputs. Sometimes I need a backing track so I can practice a part. Sometimes I want the isolated vocal to hear a harmony I keep missing. I get both files from the same upload, which is the part that made me stop juggling two different utilities. The separation runs on a Mel-Band RoFormer model. I am not going to pretend I follow every paper in that family, but I can hear the difference from the old "delete the center channel" trick. A typical three-minute song has come back for me in well under a minute, and I can send MP3, WAV, M4A, FLAC, OGG, or even a video file, up to ten minutes. The billing is in credits, at one credit per minute, and the site has given me a small bundle of free credits to try it. Files are treated as private and are set to be deleted after seven days, which is what I want for a track I do not plan to leave sitting on someone else's disk. I use it in the browser, on a laptop and sometimes on my phone, with nothing to install. The same family of pages covers a vocal isolator, an acapella extractor, an instrumental maker, a karaoke maker, a stem splitter, and a music remover. I usually stay on the main vocal remover because that is the job I actually have: one song in, two tracks out. I listen to the instrumental first to see whether the voice left a ghost, then I check the vocal for leftover drums. If a busy mix smears a bit, I try a cleaner source file before I assume the model is the problem. I do not use it as a replacement for a multitrack session I already have. I use it when all I have is the finished song and I still need a usable split. That is a common situation for me, and vocalremover.cc is the page I open for it.

title: Solving Exact Equal-Gap Board & Batten / Wainscoting Wall Spacing to 1/16" in TypeScript
summary: Anyone who has laid out a board-and-batten accent wall or wainscoting run knows the classic jobsite trap: you pick a tidy 16-inch spacer block, nail battens from left to right, and arrive at the far corner with an awkward 3-1/2-inch sliver that ruins the entire elevation. Worse, if you lay out purely by nominal lumber labels ( 1x3 or 1x4 ) instead of actual dressed US dimensions ( 2.5" or 3.5" ), cumulative rounding error throws off your centerline marks by more than an inch across a 14-foot wall. When we built the PlanCaliber Board & Batten Spacing Calculator , we wanted a deterministic TypeScript solver that behaves like a finish carpenter: solving strictly equal clear gaps down to the nearest 1/16" , printing cumulative tape-measure layout marks from 0" so small spacer errors never compound, generating an 8-foot or 12-foot board cut list, and flagging NEC 314.20 electrical box-extender requirements before the first brad nail is shot. 1. Nominal vs. Actual US Trim Widths In US lumberyards, a 1x3 pine or MDF trim board is never 3 inches wide. Every equal-gap solver must map nominal profiles to exact dressed widths in decimal inches: export type BattenProfileKey = '1x2' | '1x3' | '1x4' | '1x6' ; export const BATTEN_WIDTH_IN : Record < BattenProfileKey , number > = { '1x2' : 1.5 , '1x3' : 2.5 , '1x4' : 3.5 , '1x6' : 5.5 , } ; For standard full-height accent walls ( 96" ceiling) with a 1x6 flat baseboard ( 5.5" ), a 1x4 top rail ( 3.5" ), and a 1x2 cap ledge ( 0.75" thick), the net vertical cut length of every batten is: const netBattenHeightIn = wallHeightIn - baseboardHeightIn - ( includeTopRail ? 3.5 : 0 ) - ( includeTopRail && includeCapLedge ? 0.75 : 0 ) ; On an 8-foot ( 96" ) wall, netBattenHeightIn comes out to 86.25" . That single check reveals an immediate purchasing detail: an 8-foot ( 96" ) board yields exactly 1 vertical batten per stick, whereas a 48" wainscot wall ( netBattenHeightIn = 38.25" ) yields 2 vertical battens per 8-foot board ( Math.floor(96 / 38.25) === 2 ) and 3 per 12-foot board ( Math.floor(144 / 38.25) === 3 ). 2. The Fencepost Formula for Equal Clear Gaps There are two valid installation conventions at the left and right wall corners: Corner battens included ( includeEndBattens = true , most common) : A batten sits flush against both the left corner ( x = 0" ) and right corner ( x = L - W ). If there are N total battens, there are B = N - 1 equal clear bays between them. Corner battens omitted ( includeEndBattens = false ) : Interior battens float inside open corner bays. If there are N battens, there are B = N + 1 equal clear bays. Given total wall length L in inches, actual batten width W , and a target clear gap G_target (commonly 14" to 18" ), we solve the integer bay count and exact clear gap without floating-point drift: export function solveEqualSpacing ( wallLengthIn : number , battenWidthIn : number , targetGapIn : number , includeEndBattens : boolean , overrideCount : number | null = null ) { let battenCount : number ; if ( overrideCount !== null && overrideCount >= 1 ) { battenCount = Math . round ( overrideCount ) ; } else if ( includeEndBattens ) { const bays = Math . max ( 1 , Math . round ( ( wallLengthIn - battenWidthIn ) / ( targetGapIn + battenWidthIn ) ) ) ; battenCount = bays + 1 ; } else { const bays = Math . max ( 2 , Math . round ( wallLengthIn / ( targetGapIn + battenWidthIn ) ) ) ; battenCount = bays - 1 ; } const bayCount = includeEndBattens ? Math . max ( 1 , battenCount - 1 ) : battenCount + 1 ; const clearGapIn = ( wallLengthIn - battenCount * battenWidthIn ) / bayCount ; const onCenterIn = clearGapIn + battenWidthIn ; return { battenCount , bayCount , clearGapIn , onCenterIn } ; } Consider a 14'-6" ( 174" ) living room wall using 1x3 ( 2.5" ) battens with corner battens and a 16" target gap: bays = Math.round((174 - 2.5) / (16 + 2.5)) = Math.round(9.27) = 9 bays battenCount = 10 vertical battens clearGapIn = (174 - 10 * 2.5) / 9 = 149 / 9 = 16.5556" (rounds to 16-9/16" ) onCenterIn = 16.5556 + 2.5 = 19.0556" If one of those battens collides with an existing wall receptacle or light switch, a single click to N - 1 ( 9 battens, 18-15/16" clear gap) or N + 1 ( 11 battens, 14-5/8" clear gap) immediately shifts every vertical rail clear of the electrical box while keeping symmetric corners. 3. Cumulative Tape-Measure Marks Rounded to 1/16 Inch Finish carpenters avoid chaining a physical spacer block across 10 bays because a 1/32" error per bay accumulates to over 1/4" by the end of the wall. Instead, pull one tape measure from the left corner ( 0" ) and mark every batten's Left Edge and Centerline from the exact floating-point coordinate, rounding only at display time: function gcd ( a : number , b : number ) : number { let x = Math . abs ( a ) ; let y = Math . abs ( b ) ; while ( y !== 0 ) { const t = x % y ; x = y ; y = t ; } return x || 1 ; } export function toSixteenthFraction ( inches : number ) : string { const roundedSixteenths = Math . round ( inches * 16 ) ; const whole = Math . floor ( roundedSixteenths / 16 ) ; const rem = roundedSixteenths % 16 ; if ( rem === 0 ) return `${whole}"` ; const d = gcd ( rem , 16 ) ; return whole === 0 ? `${rem / d}/${16 / d}"` : `${whole}-${rem / d}/${16 / d}"` ; } Because each mark is computed directly from i * onCenterIn (or clearGapIn + i * onCenterIn when corner battens are omitted), rounding error never exceeds 1/32" anywhere on the wall. You can preview the live scaled elevation SVG and printable tape-measure table inside our Board & Batten Spacing Calculator . 4. Board Cut Lists, Caulk Tubes, and Stud Alignment Once battenCount and netBattenHeightIn are locked, calculating exact shopping quantities prevents mid-weekend hardware store runs: Stock boards : Divide stockLengthFt * 12 by netBattenHeightIn using Math.floor(...) (you cannot splice two vertical offcuts seamlessly into one full-height batten), then apply your waste factor ( 10% standard, 15% for knotty pine). Paintable acrylic caulk : Every vertical batten has two vertical seams against the drywall, plus horizontal seams along the top rail and baseboard. Dividing total seam linear feet by 25 LF per 10.1 oz tube gives a realistic caulk count. 16-inch OC stud check : Flagging which batten centerlines land within +/- 0.75" of standard 16" on-center stud bays tells the installer where nails hit solid framing versus where construction adhesive and opposing angled brads are needed. 5. The NEC 314.20 Electrical Box Extender Rule One of the most overlooked code details on interior wall paneling and thick wood trim is NEC 314.20 (Flush-Mounted Installations). While boxes in non-combustible drywall may sit up to 1/4" behind the finished surface, in walls or ceilings constructed of wood or other combustible surface material, boxes must sit strictly flush with the finished surface or project therefrom . If you apply 3/4" battens or MDF panel backing around an existing electrical outlet or switch, install a UL-listed box extender so the receptacle yoke seats flush with the combustible trim face rather than buried behind wood. If you are planning a full room remodel alongside your wall trim, pair the elevation takeoff with our Interior Paint & Wall Area Calculator , Drywall Sheet & Mud Calculator , and NEC 210.52 Electrical Outlet Spacing Calculator . Disclaimer: Outputs are for preliminary space planning, finish-trim layout, and material estimating only. Always verify wall dimensions, stud locations, plumb/level tolerances, and local electrical/building code requirements on site prior to cutting or installation. title: Shopify App Webhooks 2026: shopify.app.toml Subscriptions, HMAC, Retries & Price-Change Events
summary: Shopify app webhooks tutorial (2026): react to store changes from your own Shopify app - subscribe in shopify.app.toml, handle products/create and products/delete in one route, verify the HMAC with authenticate.webhook, save every event with Prisma, survive retries without duplicates, and use the new filtered events that only fire when a price changes, on a real development store. Shopify app development series, episode 9 - everything shown is real, nothing skipped. What you'll learn App-specific webhook subscriptions in shopify.app.toml authenticate.webhook: HMAC check, topic, payload, eventId Save events with Prisma and answer fast Retries: same eventId, no duplicates [events]: only when a variant price changes, with your own query Test with shopify app webhook trigger 💻 Free source code for this episode: https://github.com/fayyaz315/shopify-app-development-2026/tree/ep09 3 quick fixes from this episode Shopify Webhook Events: Only When the Price Changes (New in 2026) Shopify webhook events (2026-10): the new [events] section in shopify.app.toml fires only when a variant's price changes on an active product - and sends the result of YOUR GraphQL query. Title change: nothing. Price change: one event, seconds later. Tested on a real store. ▶ 60-second video: https://youtube.com/shorts/4znfoEHRx0E Shopify Webhooks Retry: My App Failed Once, Shopify Sent It Again Shopify webhooks retry (2026-10): my handler answered 500 on purpose, and Shopify sent the same event again within seconds - same X-Shopify-Event-Id. Save by eventId and you count deliveries instead of saving duplicates. ▶ 60-second video: https://youtube.com/shorts/PR96zt2JesU Shopify App Toml Webhooks: Subscribe Without an API Call Shopify app toml webhooks (2026-10): three lines in shopify.app.toml subscribe your app to products/create and products/delete on every store that installs it - no webhookSubscriptionCreate call. That's also why the webhookSubscriptions query returns an empty list. ▶ 60-second video: https://youtube.com/shorts/lZu89oPRc_k Step by step Preview + intro ( 0:00 ) In the next ten minutes, your app will hear about every product change in the store, a second after it happens. You'll make it fail on purpose, and watch Shopify send the same event again, and you'll see a fake webhook bounce right off. This is a Shopify app webhook at work. I create a product, and a second later, Shopify tells our app about it. This is episode nine of the Shopify app development series. Last time we built size guides with metaobjects. Today: webhooks. The full code is free on GitHub, and the link is in the description. What a webhook is ( 0:36 ) First, what a webhook is, and why you want one. Without webhooks, your app has to keep asking Shopify: did anything change? Most of the time the answer is no, and you still pay for the call. With a webhook, Shopify tells you once, the moment something happens. Good uses: sync products to another system, clear a cache, send an alert, or clean up when a merchant uninstalls your app. Here's the path. Something changes in the store. Shopify sends a signed POST request to a URL in your app. Your app checks the signature, saves what it needs, and answers two hundred, fast. If it doesn't, Shopify tries again. Subscribe in shopify.app.toml ( 1:18 ) In 2026, you subscribe in shopify.app.toml. No API call, no setup code. The template already has two: app uninstalled, and scopes update. I add one more subscription. One URI, slash webhooks/catalog, and two topics: products create and products delete. When you run shopify app dev, or deploy, the CLI sends these subscriptions to Shopify with the app. They belong to your app, on every store that installs it. The URI is a path. Shopify puts your app's URL in front of it, so it follows your tunnel during development. The template's app uninstalled handler is a good first example. It deletes the shop's sessions, and it's written to run twice safely. For apps with heavy traffic, a subscription can also point at Google Pub Sub or Amazon EventBridge instead of a URL. The handler: HMAC first ( 2:15 ) Now the handler. The path/webhooks/catalog means a route file named webhooks.catalog. It only has an action, because Shopify always sends a POST. The first line is authenticate.webhook. That one call checks the HMAC signature. Shopify signs every body with your app's secret. A request without a valid signature never gets past this line. The signature is in the X Shopify H mac header: a hash of the raw body, made with your app's client secret. That's why the helper reads the raw body itself. It gives back the topic, the shop, the payload, and two IDs: the webhook ID, and the event ID. One URL, two topics, so I switch on the topic. Create sends the whole product, so I keep the title and the status. Delete sends only the ID. Topics arrive in capitals with underscores, like products underscore create. The create payload is the full product, in the older REST shape: handle, body HTML, variants, and admin graphql api id, the GraphQL ID for follow-up queries. On delete, the product is already gone, so the ID is all you get. If you need more, keep your own copy when it's created. Then I answer with an empty response, which means two hundred. Shopify waits about five seconds, so slow work belongs in a queue, not here. Save every event ( 3:41 ) Every event is saved in the app's own database, so the page can show it later. The event ID is the primary key, and there's a deliveries counter that starts at one. Why? Shopify can deliver the same event more than once. So save event is an upsert by event ID. A new event creates a row. The same event again only adds one to deliveries. No duplicate rows, no double work. The Webhooks page ( 4:07 ) And a new Webhooks page to watch it all. The loader reads the latest twenty events for this shop from our table. Webhooks arrive in the background, so the page re-reads the list every three seconds. The table shows the topic, what happened, when Shopify triggered it, when we received it, and the deliveries count. The buttons make real changes in the store, with the GraphQL mutations from earlier episodes. So every webhook you'll see is real. One detail from testing. The page keeps the new product's ID and finds it by ID, because product search lags a few seconds behind a brand new product. Here's the page. Six buttons that change the store, and an empty list of received events. Live: create and rename ( 4:50 ) Create test product. Products create. It reached our app about a second after the change: Created Webhook test tee, active. And a second event too. We'll come back to that one in a moment. Now, change its title. The title changed in Shopify, and nothing arrives. We didn't subscribe to product updates, so we don't get them. Two times on every row. Triggered is when the change happened in Shopify. Received is when it reached us. Here, under a second apart. Price-change events ( 5:20 ) Here's the new part. Most apps don't care about every update, only about one thing. Like a price. The events section of the toml does that. Topic product, action update, and triggers: the variant's price and compareAtPrice. Then your own GraphQL query. Shopify runs it and sends you the result, not the whole product. And a query filter: only active products. Change its price. One event: Webhook test tee v2, price five. With the new title, because the payload is the result of our query. That second event on create was this one. A new product's variant gets its first price, zero, and that counts as a price change. The handler is the same style. authenticate.webhook, then the data from our query: the product and the variant. Retries: fail on purpose ( 6:13 ) Now the part most tutorials skip: what happens when your app fails. Fail the next delivery. It writes a small flag file. The handler sees the flag on a first delivery, deletes it, and answers five hundred. Delete it. Products delete. Saved, but we answered five hundred. Deliveries: one. A few seconds later, Shopify sends it again. Same event ID, so the same row. Deliveries: two. If your app keeps failing, Shopify keeps trying. Its docs say up to eight times over four hours, so a short outage doesn't lose events. That's why the event ID matters. Without the upsert, this product would have been deleted twice in our data. So, make your handler safe to run twice. Shopify promises at least one delivery, not exactly one. A fake webhook: 401 ( 7:02 ) Last button. Anyone can find your webhook URL and post to it. Send a fake webhook. Refused, four oh one. The headers look real, but the signature isn't, because we don't have Shopify's secret. The fake request sets every Shopify header. Only the HMAC is made up, and that's enough to stop it. In my tests, a request without Shopify's headers got four hundred. A GET request too. Only a real, signed POST gets through. Where are my subscriptions? ( 7:34 ) One more thing that confused me at first. In GraphiQL, I ask for the app's webhook subscriptions. An empty list. Our toml subscriptions are working, but this query doesn't show them. That query lists subscriptions made with the API, for one store. Toml subscriptions are app specific, so you manage them in the toml, not with this query. You'd only use that API when one store needs something different, for example a webhook that depends on a merchant's settings. To test a handler without touching the store, the CLI has shopify app webhook trigger. It sends a signed sample, an example T-shirt. In my test it arrived, signed and valid, but for a different shop domain, so our page, which filters by shop, didn't list it. Honest notes ( 8:21 ) A few honest notes before the recap. One: the fail button uses a file on disk. Fine for a demo. In a real app, never fail on purpose. Two: we do the work inside the request. A real app with slow work should save the event, answer, and process it in a queue. Three: webhooks can arrive out of order. Use the triggered at time, not the arrival time, if order matters. Want to practise? Subscribe to collections create, and show new collections on the same page. And everything you saw was tested on my real development store, on API version 2026-10, before I pressed record. Recap ( 9:02 ) So, the recap. Subscribe in shopify.app.toml: topics in the webhooks section, and only the changes you need in the events section. Start every handler with authenticate.webhook, so a fake request gets four oh one. Save by event ID, because Shopify retries, and the same event can come twice. And answer fast. Slow work goes in a queue. That's Shopify app webhooks in 2026, inside a real app, on a real store. The full code for this episode is free on GitHub. The link is in the description. Next episode: files and media. Your app uploads images to Shopify, and adds them to products. See you there. 📖 The full written tutorial with every episode: https://www.wixob.com/shopify-app-webhook-tutorial/ 📚 Course page: https://www.wixob.com/shopify-app-development-2026/ 🔔 New episodes on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@fayyaz-ahmed-shopify-developer?sub_confirmation=1 Questions about the Shopify GraphQL Admin API? Ask in the comments — I answer every one.

title: A walker, a horse, a car and a flying ray: movement in a WebGL2 engine where everything is code
summary: Before version 0.8.0 a figure in Wallhammer Web could walk on a flat test course. It started and stopped in one frame, turned on the spot at any speed, and could not stand on the planet the engine draws. Now the same figure walks on that planet, hands a box to a second figure, rides a four-legged runner at a gallop, drives a car over a ramp and flies a huge ray that pants after it lands. This is an account of what was added in versions 0.8.0 and 0.8.2, and of the reason behind each piece. Wallhammer Web is a 3D engine for the browser where everything is written in code: plain WebGL2, no graphics library, no model files, no textures. Every animal and car in the pictures is a function. Why movement, and why now The engine could already make a world: a planet you can fly down to, rivers, a village, an endless streamed land. What it could not do was let you be in that world as something with weight. A camera that flies is a viewer. A body that needs four metres to stop is a game. So the goal of these two versions was one sentence: every way of moving that a small open world needs, as engine parts a game configures, never as code of one example. The examples only prove the parts work. Three rules held through all of it: Fixed steps, same bits. Every body advances in fixed steps. Cut the same seconds into frames of 30, 60 or 144 Hz and the body ends in the same place with the same bits. Every body saves and loads its state. Every number is a setup field. The engine ships a reference set and the game replaces it. No constant of one car hides in the step. A check for every behaviour. Stop distances, turning circles, sink rates and footfalls are measured by scenarios that run headless. There are 151 of them for walking, riding, driving and flying, and 64 for motion. 0.8.0: a walker with momentum, on a sphere Momentum The walker got three numbers: braking on the ground, a slower run-up, and a turn rate that falls with speed. A runner now stops in v² / (2 · deceleration) metres and turns in an arc instead of on a coin. All three default to zero, so every existing game steps bit for bit as before. That is a pattern for the whole release: new behaviour is off until asked for. On top of that sit movement profiles in the examples ( default , heavy , light ), a gait that leans into the run-up and back against braking, and ChainLag , a small spring chain for things that trail behind a body. The figure's ponytail is three bones of it. Walking on a sphere without a sphere walker The planet is a sphere of 100 km radius. Writing a second walker for curved ground would mean two walkers to keep equal for ever. Instead the flat walker and the flat collision world run unchanged inside a chart : a flat map of the ground round an anchor (the exponential map). Within a few hundred metres the error is far under a millimetre. When the body walks away, the chart moves under it at a step boundary, and the camera is carried across so the picture does not move. The trees and rocks in that picture are instances of streamed cells, drawn by the thousand. They now also stop the walker and the camera's boom: each archetype says in plain data where its solid footprint is, and an index answers "what is solid within this radius" without allocating. Hands that reach The handover above needs more than a played clip, because the two figures never stand in the same place twice. TwoBoneReach moves a hand to a target set every frame, with a soft pull so nothing pops when the target is out of reach. ChainAim turns a head and chest toward a point. Sockets carry a held thing from one hand to another over set seconds. The order in a frame is fixed: the ground fit, aims, reaches, sockets. 0.8.2: four legs, four wheels, two wings Steps of several legs A four-legged animal cannot use a walk cycle made for two legs, and three hand-made clips (walk, trot, gallop) slide their feet whenever the speed sits between them. StepCycle takes the gaits as data instead: per leg an offset in the cycle, how long it stays down, how high it lifts, and a stride. const patterns : StepPattern [ ] = [ { speed : 0.8 , stride : 0.9 , offsets : [ 0 , 0.5 , 0.75 , 0.25 ] , duty : 0.75 , lift : 0.08 } , // one leg at a time { speed : 2.5 , stride : 1.6 , offsets : [ 0 , 0.5 , 0.5 , 0 ] , duty : 0.5 , lift : 0.12 } , // diagonal pairs { speed : 6 , stride : 2.8 , offsets : [ 0 , 0.1 , 0.55 , 0.65 ] , duty : 0.35 , lift : 0.16 } , // a bound with a flight ] ; const steps = new StepCycle ( { homes , patterns , reach : 0.5 } ) ; The cycle is driven by the distance travelled, not by time. A planted foot does not move until it lifts. A swing lands where the ground will be. The patterns blend by speed with their offsets on a circle, so a walk becomes a trot without a jump. The check of the ray's crawl measures the drift of its planted paws: 0.00 mm a step. A body carried by another The rider is not a second animation glued on. SocketSeat gives the root of one body from a socket on another, with a weight from 0 (where the game put it) to 1 (in the seat), and a share of the mount's tilt. Hands and feet are held at sockets on the reins and the rug with the same reach as the handover. A wheeled body WheeledBody is one rigid body on wheel rays: springs and dampers, tyres with a slip curve and a friction circle, a handbrake that lets the rear slide, steering that eases with speed, and a hull of spheres that does not pass through thin walls. const body = new WheeledBody ( world , { mass : 1100 , wheels : fourWheels ( { drive : 'all' , frontGrip : 0.95 } ) , } ) ; const intent = newWheeledIntent ( ) ; intent . throttle = 1 ; intent . steer = 0.3 ; body . advance ( dt , intent ) ; // the fixed steps due; the rest of dt waits for the next frame body . renderMatrix ( pose ) ; // between the last two steps A raycast car is easy to get driving and hard to get right at rest, so most of its scenarios are about the dull cases: parked on a slope of 15° it settles within a centimetre and stays; it sleeps and wakes; a walker is blocked by it. A flying body, and the assist that makes it playable FlyingBody crawls on the ground, leaps, and in the air is a glider with one lift coefficient: lift and drag from a trim speed and a glide ratio, banked turns with a load limit, a stall, beats that push, a flare. It flew correctly and nobody could fly it. Holding height meant pumping two keys, and every slow turn ended in a stall. The first idea was to soften the physics. I kept the physics and added FlightAssist instead: the player asks for a speed, a climb and a turn, and the assist writes the body's raw controls before every step by inverting the body's own model . Hands off, it holds speed and height. It reaches a new speed in about two seconds, turns level, never stalls and lands from a slow descent. With assist=0 the raw controls are still there. One mechanism for getting on The horse and the car first had their own code for getting on and off. They are now two configurations of one SeatTransition : an approach, a seat weight and a rise eased per phase, with cues at times (the door opens, the hand takes the rein). The engine also answers where a body may stand when it gets off, so nobody dismounts into a wall. Traces on the ground A world that takes no mark from you feels like a backdrop. ContactTrail keeps marks in a ring of fixed size and draws them in one instanced draw; only the changed span is uploaded each frame. Boot prints, hoof prints, ruts and skid marks share it. Particle bursts are fired once from a seed and simulated in the vertex shader, and the ground carries a surface tag so a wheel knows it is on loose dirt. The animals are code too The runner and the ray have no model file. Each is a function that builds a skinned mesh from numbers, and that makes small life cheap to add: a jaw, a tongue, eyelids and a few named random streams give panting after a gallop, a yawn, a lick and a blink. The streams are seeded, so the same seed yawns at the same moment on every machine. What is still weak A body on a car has no weight. The walker is a capsule without mass, so the car does not sink when somebody gets in, and nobody can stand on its roof. That is the next piece of work: a force at a point and a payload for the wheeled body, then a car that meets a walker, then moving ground for the walker. The ray's wing on the ground is a flat plank. It should fold like a fan, and that needs a third joint in the arm. The rider sits still. At a gallop the body should move with the mount. There is no adaptive resolution. A frame of the village costs 3.4 ms on an M4 Pro at 1600×900, but the dust of the destruction example costs 2.9 ms for about two thousand triangles, all of it overdraw. Quality tiers and cheaper dust are on the list. There is no 0.8.1. Its release failed in CI on two faults that never show locally: a time limit of 5 s that the walking scenarios missed by 0.2 s on the slower CI machine, and a file permission in a job that ran in CI for the first time. Nothing reached npm, the fixes went in, and the changes shipped as 0.8.2. Try it Live: the movement course . E gets on and off the runner, the cars and the ray. On the planet , G drops you to the ground. The engine: Wallhammer Web on GitHub , npm install wallhammer-web , MIT licensed. About 67 thousand lines of TypeScript, 1.3 MB as an npm package, and one runtime dependency ( earcut , for triangulation). The full list: the changelog names every new export of both versions. If you have written a raycast car or a quadruped gait and know where mine will break, I would like to hear it.

title: My Swift terminal games play themselves. Press an arrow key to take over, in your browser
summary: NeNe Swarm is a fixed-screen shooter, and NeNe Bolt is a side-scrolling platformer. In both, an AI plays forever. Press an arrow key and the game is yours from that frame on; leave the keys alone for 30 seconds and the AI takes over again. They are written in Swift for the Linux terminal, and both also run in the browser. Open hideyuki-mori.com on a computer with a keyboard (a phone has no arrow keys), click the swarm or bolt icon on the site's desktop, click inside the window and press an arrow key. Swarm (fixed shooter) Bolt (side-scroller) Move ← → ← → Climb ladders — ↑ ↓ Jump — Z or Space (hold for higher) Fire Space or Z X (hold to charge) Theme / difficulty / quit t / d / q t / d / q While you are playing, the HUD says so ( YOU AI IN 27 in Swarm, PLAYER 30s in Bolt) and counts down to the moment the AI takes the controls back. How a terminal game hears a key being released In Bolt, hold → and the runner keeps running; let go and it stops on that frame. That isn't a given in a terminal. Hold → in most terminals and the program gets a stream of repeated arrow sequences; let go and it gets nothing. Windows Terminal has a mode for this. When the game writes ESC [ ? 9001 h at startup, the terminal switches to win32-input-mode, and every press and every release arrives as its own sequence, ESC [ Vk ; Sc ; Uc ; Kd ; Cs ; Rc _ , where Kd says whether the key went down or up. These sequences pass through to programs running inside WSL, so the game knows exactly which keys are held on each frame. On exit it writes ESC [ ? 9001 l before restoring the screen. In other terminals the games fall back to key repeats: a key counts as held for 0.6 seconds after it arrives and then for as long as the repeats keep coming, so the runner can overshoot a little. In the browser it's simple again, since keydown and keyup give the same information as win32-input-mode. The game never reads the clock The game itself is a pure function: the current state, the buttons held on this frame and a seeded random source give the next state. Only the outermost layer reads the time, the keys and the seed. Your keys and the AI's decisions become the same set of buttons and go through the same function. Positions are integers (one cell is 16 units), and on screen the ships, runner, enemies, shots and terrain are blocks of color two terminal columns wide, so one "pixel" comes out roughly square. That is what made the browser versions checkable. They are TypeScript ports, written with Claude Code like the Swift originals, and I don't take a port's word for it: each one replays the same seeds and the same scripted key presses as the Swift code, renders every frame at two terminal sizes, and compares a hash of each frame's characters and colors with what Swift produced. The random generator is the same SplitMix64 on both sides, done in exact integer arithmetic. Swarm's port matches on 240,008 frames, including a script where a human cuts in four times and lets the AI take back over four times. Bolt's matches on 258,010. So when you take the controls on the site, you are playing the same game the Swift binary runs. Try Swarm or Bolt at hideyuki-mori.com and see how long you last before the AI gets them back. Installing the terminal version Each game has a one-line installer for Linux x86_64 (WSL2 on Windows works). For Swarm: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hideyukiMORI/nene-swarm/main/install.sh | bash It checks the 2.7 MB download against SHA256SUMS and installs one binary in ~/.local/bin . The Swift standard library is linked in, so all you need is glibc 2.35 or newer. From PowerShell, install.ps1 in the same repository runs it inside WSL. Bolt and Swarm have six siblings, all in Swift and open source: Gambit (four AIs trade insults over chess), Igo (the same on a 19×19 Go board), Wire (a news ticker), Reversi , Poker and Sand (pour sand with the mouse). Gambit, Igo and Wire run on the site too, to watch rather than play. The sources of the two you can play: nene-swarm and nene-bolt . ── Hideyuki Mori 🔗 hideyuki-mori.com

title: PSNR over white and edge alpha error disagreed about which transparent PNG was better
summary: If you judge a palette-reduced transparent PNG by PSNR over a white background, the number can rank samples in a different order than their edges do. A pair of measurements that tracks the edge more directly is the average alpha error over only the pixels that were semi-transparent in the source, plus a count of how many of them ended up fully opaque or fully transparent. On three samples reduced to 64 colors with pngquant 3.0.3 and dithering off, the edge errors were 2.65, 0.71 and 2.42 alpha levels, while PSNR over white read 43.2, 52.4 and 55.1 dB. The two lists do not sort the same way, and that is the whole reason to report both. All three samples are self-made, generated by a script with fictional content, 800×800 RGBA each. Generated samples are flatter than real design files. Everything below is one run on one Apple-silicon Mac, so read each figure as "on these samples". How the edge error is counted Take every pixel whose source alpha is strictly between 0 and 255. For each one, compute the absolute difference between the source alpha and the output alpha, on the 0–255 scale, and average. That is the edge alpha error. The second measurement is a count. Of the semi-transparent pixels in the source, how many became exactly 255, and how many became exactly 0. An average of 2.5 levels can hide a lot of pixels that jumped to opaque, so the count tells you which way the error leans. What the three samples gave T1 is a feathered circle with a soft edge about 28 px wide. T2 is a rounded card with a dark offset shadow. T3 is a triangle and lettering with only a 1 px antialiased edge. The share of semi-transparent pixels is computed here by dividing their pixel counts by 640,000, not a separate measurement. Sample Semi-transparent pixels Share of image 256 colors: error / PSNR 64 colors: error / PSNR T1 feathered 230,502 36.0% 1.20 / 49.4 dB 2.65 / 43.2 dB T2 shadow 142,722 22.3% 0.03 / 65.1 dB 0.71 / 52.4 dB T3 hard edge 12,954 2.0% 0.77 / 63.3 dB 2.42 / 55.1 dB Error is in alpha levels over the source semi-transparent pixels, PSNR is computed after compositing on white, and dithering is off in every row. Measured, reading the table in order: going from 256 to 64 colors multiplied the feathered edge error by about 2.2, while the shadow's error moved by under one level (0.03 to 0.71), since a shadow is one color at many opacities. At 64 colors T3 has a higher edge error than T2 (2.42 against 0.71) but a higher PSNR (55.1 against 52.4 dB). At 256 colors the order agrees again (T3 at 0.77 and 63.3 dB, T2 at 0.03 and 65.1 dB), but the error differs about 25-fold (0.77 against 0.03) while PSNR differs by under 2 dB. Where the semi-transparent pixels went Measured on T1, pngquant never pushed a semi-transparent pixel to fully transparent. It did push some to fully opaque: 10,216 at 256 colors, 16,443 at 64 colors with dithering, and 19,482 at 64 colors without. On T2 at 64 colors without dithering, 1,176 pixels went to opaque and the maximum error was 32 levels. Switching dithering on barely moved the average error on T1 (3.05 against 2.65). Two cruder reductions look very different. Forcing alpha to two values, a hard 0 or 255 split at 128, gave an average error of 39.2 on T1, 25.1 on T2 and 20.9 on T3, with no semi-transparent pixel left. On the shadow sample 139,901 pixels went fully transparent, so the shadow vanished. Pillow's FASTOCTREE at 64 colors gave 7.60, 6.7 and 4.4, and it turned every originally opaque pixel slightly translucent (alpha 248 to 253 on T1, 254 on T2 and T3). No PSNR was taken for either of these, so how they would score over white is unknown. Why PSNR over white hides most of it This part is inference and was not measured separately. There are two likely causes, and the sample table is consistent with both. First, PSNR averages over all 640,000 pixels, and the semi-transparent ones are only 2.0% of T3 and 22.3% of T2. An error confined to a thin band gets diluted by a large area that is exactly right. Second, composited on white, an alpha error is scaled by how far the pixel color is from white. A light or low-opacity edge pixel can be wrong in alpha and still land close to white. On a dark background the same error would show up differently, and that was not measured. If that reading is right, the practical rule is to report the edge error and the opaque and transparent counts next to PSNR, and to composite on the background the asset will really sit on. One way around the whole problem If the edge has to stay exact, palette PNG was the wrong container on these samples. Lossless WebP kept alpha identical on the feathered sample, 0 differing pixels, at 45,314 bytes against the 126,939-byte original. The feathered and shadow samples also went through ImgIng https://imging.ai/ in a desktop browser. It picked WebP by default (quality 84, a lossy setting) and their edge error came out at 0; colour was not compared pixel by pixel. Not checked here: real design files, other quantizers, other background colors, and PSNR for the two-level and octree outputs.

title: Node fetch proxy: ProxyAgent, env vars, SOCKS5 and auth
summary: Originally published on proxymint . Send Node's built-in fetch through a proxy: undici ProxyAgent, NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY, encoded auth, SOCKS5, rotation and the errors each mistake throws. TL;DR Pass a ProxyAgent as the dispatcher. fetch(url, { dispatcher: new ProxyAgent(" http://USERNAME:PASSWORD@HOST:PORT" ) }) routes HTTP and HTTPS through the proxy. Import fetch and ProxyAgent from the same undici package. Built-in fetch ignores HTTP_PROXY by default. Node reads the proxy variables only with NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 or --use-env-proxy, available from Node 24.0.0 and 22.21.0. The undici versions must match. An npm undici 8 ProxyAgent passed to the built-in fetch on Node 22 or 24 fails with invalid onRequestStart method; on Node 22, importing undici 8 also switches the environment proxy off without an error. Encode credentials or pass a token. A raw / or # in the password makes the ProxyAgent constructor throw invalid url; encodeURIComponent each part or use the token option. Use undici 7.28.0 or 8.2.0 and later for SOCKS5. Socks5ProxyAgent arrived in 7.23.0, but releases before the fix can send a request to the wrong origin (CVE-2026-6734). It takes socks5:// URLs, sends host names to the proxy, and is marked experimental. Key takeaways Check process.versions.undici before copying ProxyAgent code. Keep the agent and fetch from one implementation, call install(), or pin the undici major your Node bundles. Walk err.cause to read proxy failures. fetch wraps them in TypeError: fetch failed, and a refused tunnel shows its 407 two causes deep. Scrub proxy URLs from logs. Node's ERR_PROXY_TUNNEL message prints the configured proxy URL with the password. Test rotation with reused and fresh agents. An agent reuses tunnels per origin, and each concurrent HTTPS request opens its own CONNECT. Set a timeout on every proxied call. Fetch has no overall timeout; pass AbortSignal.timeout() and retry 429, 5xx and timeouts, never 407 or 403. Read the full guide on proxymint , with the commands, tables and sources.

title: Disk full? Find what's eating your space with df, du and sort (Linux)
summary: AI disclosure: this article was created with the help of AI. An AI assistant drafted the text from the lesson script, and it was reviewed before publishing. Every command was actually run in a fresh debian:13 container (GNU coreutils 9.7); all outputs below are copied from that run, not written by hand. A step-by-step way to find what's filling a Linux disk: check the filesystem with df -h, drill down with du -sh and du --max-depth piped into sort -h, list the biggest files with find -size, empty a log safely with truncate, and solve the classic mystery where df says the disk is full but du can't find the files (a deleted file that's still open). The problem: No space left on device. Your app stops writing, your database refuses to start, and you need to know what's filling the disk, fast. Step 1: which filesystem is full? df -h Start with df. It reports space per filesystem, and -h prints sizes in human units. $ df -h /lab Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on overlay 59G 21G 36G 37% / In a container you see the overlay filesystem. On a server you'd look for the line with a high use percentage, usually the one mounted on slash, or on slash var. df answers which disk is full. It can't tell you which files. That's the job of du. Step 2: which folder? du -sh du -sh gives one total per argument. With a star, that's one line per folder here. $ du -sh * 93M app 205M backups 3.1M uploads Backups is clearly the biggest. But sorting by eye doesn't scale, so let's let the computer sort. Step 3: drill down with --max-depth and sort -h --max-depth=2 shows totals two levels deep, and sort -h understands human sizes, so ten megabytes sorts before one gigabyte. $ du -h --max-depth=2 . | sort -h 3.1M ./uploads 25M ./app/cache 69M ./app/logs 93M ./app 205M ./backups 300M . The biggest are at the bottom. Plain sort, without -h , would compare the text and put a hundred megabytes before nine megabytes. To see the top offenders, files included, add -a and reverse the sort. $ du -ah . | sort -rh | head -6 300M . 205M ./backups 104M ./backups/db-2026-11.sql.gz 100M ./backups/db-2026-10.sql.gz 93M ./app 69M ./app/logs Step 4: list the big files with find If you already know what's big for you, find can list every file above a size, here fifty megabytes, wherever it is. $ find . -type f -size +50M -exec ls -lh { } + -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 60M Nov 21 19:39 ./app/logs/app.log.1 -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 100M Nov 21 19:39 ./backups/db-2026-10.sql.gz -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 104M Nov 21 19:39 ./backups/db-2026-11.sql.gz Two database dumps and a rotated log. These are the usual suspects on a real server: old backups, logs and caches. Step 5: free space safely To empty a log that a program may still be writing, don't delete it. truncate -s 0 cuts it to zero bytes, and the file stays in place. $ truncate -s 0 app/logs/app.log.1 && du -sh app 33M app Be careful with this on files you might need: the content is gone for good. For old backups, move them somewhere else before you delete anything. The mystery: df says full, du disagrees One more case that confuses everyone. Let's create a big temporary file. $ fallocate -l 200M big.tmp && du -sh . 440M . Now a process opens it and keeps it open. Here that's just sleep, reading from the file in the background. $ sleep 600 < big.tmp & And someone deletes the file to free space. $ rm big.tmp && du -sh . 240M . The file is gone from the folder, so du doesn't count it. But the process still holds it open, so the space is not freed, and df still shows it as used. To find such files, look for open file handles marked deleted in slash proc. $ find /proc/*/fd -lname '*(deleted)' -printf '%p -> %l\n' 2 > /dev/null /proc/120/fd/0 - > /lab/srv/big.tmp ( deleted ) The number in the path is the process I D. Stopping or restarting that process releases the space. $ kill %1 The trap, in one paragraph I deleted a 200 MB file, but df still counts the space as used. What is the likely cause? The space comes back only when that process closes the file, or is restarted. Quick check 1. After du -h, why sort -h and not plain sort? sort -h is faster sort -h understands sizes like 9M and 100M sort -h sorts by folder name Answer sort -h understands sizes like 9M and 100M : Plain sort compares text, so a hundred megabytes would land before nine megabytes. 2. I deleted a 200 MB file, but df still counts the space as used. What is the likely cause? The disk is damaged A process still has the deleted file open du skips hidden files Answer A process still has the deleted file open : The space comes back only when that process closes the file, or is restarted. Recap df -h tells you which filesystem is full. du -sh and du --max-depth , piped into sort -h , tell you which folder. find -size lists the big files, truncate -s 0 empties a live log, and if df and du disagree, look for deleted files that are still open. Source and reproducible setup Lesson page with the same quiz (and a video version): https://shellprovenai.github.io/lekcje/disk-space-df-du/ Commands, demo setup script and full test log: https://github.com/shellprovenai/terminal-tutorials/tree/main/disk-space-df-du This article was created with the help of AI and reviewed before publishing. The video on the lesson page uses AI narration and AI-generated robot-and-dog presenters. No sponsors, no affiliate links.

title: Dithering a feathered PNG to 64 colours made it 3.5x bigger, not more accurate
summary: When a soft-edged transparent PNG gets squeezed into 64 colours, does turning dithering on fix the edge? On the feathered sample below it did not: the edge error stayed almost where it was and the file came out 3.5 times larger. Every number here is tagged measured , inference or not tested , so you can see which is which. The samples and the yardstick Three transparent PNGs, all generated by a script, all 800×800, all fictional. A feathered orange-to-purple circle (126,939 B, 230,502 semi-transparent pixels), a rounded card with a drop shadow (28,596 B) and a triangle logo with a 1 px anti-aliased edge (58,744 B). Generated art has a lot of flat colour, so it compresses more easily than a real design file. Read the percentages as relative. The tool is pngquant 3.0.3, one run per setting on one Apple-silicon Mac (measured). The error metric is the mean edge alpha error on a 0–255 scale, counted only over pixels that were semi-transparent in the original (measured definition). Edge error follows the colour count Feathered sample, dithering on versus off (all measured): Colours Dither Size (B) Edge alpha error 256 on 43,434 1.27 256 off 26,438 1.20 128 on 49,084 2.00 128 off 19,650 1.81 64 on 51,349 3.05 64 off 14,854 2.65 Going from 256 to 64 colours roughly doubled the error, 1.20–1.27 up to 2.65–3.05 (measured). Switching dithering on or off at the same colour count moved it by 0.4 at most (measured). File size follows dithering At 64 colours the dithered feathered file is 51,349 B and the undithered one is 14,854 B, so 3.5x (measured). At 256 colours the gap is 1.6x (measured). With dithering on, the 128 and 64 colour files are both bigger than the 256 colour one, which looks backwards; a plausible reason is that fewer palette entries need more noise to hide the steps (inference, the encoder internals were not checked). The undithered 64 colour file also pushed slightly more near-opaque edge pixels to fully opaque, 19,482 against 16,443 (measured). No pixel in either file became fully transparent (measured). The other two samples barely care At 64 colours the shadow card was 10,409 B dithered and 9,214 B undithered, with errors of 0.70 and 0.71 (measured). The hard-edge logo was 13,041 B against 11,472 B, errors 2.43 and 2.42 (measured). Both stay within 14% on size. The 3.5x jump only shows up on the feathered sample (measured), so check your own soft-edged assets before generalising. What the dithered edge looks like Zoomed to 3x on a checkerboard, the undithered 64 colour feathered circle shows visible steps along the fade, and the dithered one swaps those for fine grain (observed in the zoomed images of these samples). The error numbers are close, so the choice is about which artefact you can live with, and the grain is the one that costs about 36,500 extra bytes (51,349 minus 14,854, calculated). When edge error is the real problem If 2–3 levels of alpha error is too much, the lever is not the dither flag. Keeping 8-bit alpha untouched gave an error of 0 on all three samples but cannot be saved as an indexed PNG (measured), and WebP lossless kept alpha identical pixel for pixel on the feathered circle at 45,314 B (measured). The browser-side comparison used ImgIng https://imging.ai/ on the same feathered sample.
